title: AI Finds Hidden Health Risks in Routine Sleep Study Data
excerpt: A Cleveland Clinic-IBM study published in Nature Communications shows AI can identify patients at twice the mortality risk from standard overnight sleep recordings that current clinical methods overlook.
body:
• A new AI model developed by Cleveland Clinic and IBM can identify long-term health risks — including heart disease, cognitive decline, and death — from routine overnight sleep studies
  • Patients in the highest-risk group had twice the mortality risk over five years compared to those in the lowest-risk group, a distinction invisible to standard sleep apnea metrics
  • Between 1 and 4 million sleep studies are performed annually in the U.S., but clinicians currently extract only a fraction of the physiological data these tests capture
  • A separate Stanford model called SleepFM can predict over 100 health conditions from a single night's sleep, with high accuracy for cancers, heart disease, and Parkinson's

More Than Just Sleep Apnea

A routine overnight sleep study captures rich data about a patient's brain, lungs, muscles, and heart. But for decades, clinicians have distilled all of that information into just a handful of summary measures — primarily to grade sleep apnea severity using a metric called the apnea-hypopnea index.

A new study published in Nature Communications suggests that approach leaves critical health signals on the table. Researchers from Cleveland Clinic, IBM, Yale, and the University of Washington developed an AI model that can extract far more from standard polysomnography data, identifying hidden patterns linked to heart disease, cognitive decline, and mortality risk.

"For decades we have distilled an overnight sleep study into a handful of summary measures. AI gives us the opportunity to move beyond those summaries and learn from the full richness of sleep physiology."

— Dr. Reena Mehra, University of Washington, Senior Clinical Author

Five Risk Groups, Sharp Differences

Using data from the Cleveland Clinic STARLIT (Sleep Signals, Testing, and Reports Linked to Patient Traits) registry, the researchers grouped patients into five risk categories. The results were stark: patients in the highest-risk group had twice the mortality risk over the next five years compared to those in the lowest-risk group.

This stratification was not captured by the apnea-hypopnea index, the standard clinical measure. The AI model also predicted outcomes equally well for men and women — a significant improvement, since the apnea-hypopnea index has historically performed better in men. The findings were independently confirmed in a nationwide patient cohort.

The model was built through the Discovery Accelerator, a 10-year joint research partnership between Cleveland Clinic and IBM focused on advancing life sciences through AI and quantum computing.

Stanford's SleepFM Adds to the Evidence

The Cleveland Clinic findings align with a separate breakthrough from Stanford Medicine. Published in Nature Medicine in January 2026, Stanford's SleepFM model was trained on nearly 600,000 hours of sleep data from 65,000 participants. It can predict a person's risk of developing more than 100 health conditions from one night's polysomnography recording.

SleepFM showed particularly high accuracy for Parkinson's disease (C-index 0.89), prostate cancer (0.89), breast cancer (0.87), dementia (0.85), heart attack (0.81), and overall death (0.84). The model was paired with up to 25 years of follow-up health records from the Stanford Sleep Medicine Center.

"SleepFM is essentially learning the language of sleep."

— James Zou, Associate Professor of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford Medicine

Why This Matters Beyond the Lab

An estimated 1 to 4 million polysomnograms are performed in the United States each year. These studies already exist in clinical workflows — the infrastructure is in place. What the AI models demonstrate is that the data already being collected contains far more diagnostic value than current practice extracts.

Nearly 70 million Americans live with chronic sleep disorders. If validated across diverse populations, these AI tools could enable earlier detection of cardiovascular disease, neurological decline, and cancers — all from a test that patients already undergo for routine sleep concerns.

The Cleveland Clinic team emphasized that the next step is validation in diverse populations and expansion of collaborations with industry partners and professional societies.

What's Next

Both research teams are working to move from proof-of-concept to clinical application. Stanford's group is exploring whether data from consumer wearables could supplement lab-based polysomnography, potentially making predictive sleep analysis accessible to millions more people. Cleveland Clinic is pursuing broader validation studies. Neither tool is intended to replace clinical expertise — rather, they would serve as aids to help sleep specialists identify risk earlier and more precisely.
